description: I'm a high school student in California who likes building things where AI, sound and accessibility meet. I use Python and am interested in measuring whether AI-generated audio and video are good, not just whether they look good on a chart. My paper evaluating AI-generated songs was accepted at a WACV 2027 workshop. I'm building a web jukebox that turns NASA Earth Information Center animations into music, letting blind and low-vision people hear sea ice shrink, fires spread and cities light up.
summary: Listen to Earth is a free web app that turns 25 NASA Earth Information Center animations into music, designed to help people who are blind or have low vision explore Earth information by ear. These visual animations show sea ice, fires, city lights, CO2 and air quality. The app reads the colours representing these features and plays them as rhythm. Each two-second bar scans eight map strips from west to east, with feature amounts controlling the number and loudness of hits. Users can play prepared soundtracks, generate sound live from an animation or their own NASA video, and explore Arctic sea-ice change through narration, touch and year-to-year comparisons. Screen-reader descriptions, keyboard controls and phone support are built in. I compared seven sound methods using automated benchmarks and listening tests with method names hidden (one listener). Rhythm won all three first-round pairings, and quantity comparisons were correct 69% of the time across rounds. Testing with blind and low-vision users is the next step.
details:
Project APP Link:

https://luckisondu.github.io/earth-information-jukebox/

Source Code:

https://github.com/LuckisonDu/earth-information-jukebox

What it does and how it works

Listen to Earth makes NASA's Earth animations audible. This free web jukebox turns 25 Earth Information Center animations from NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio into music. It runs in modern phone and computer browsers without installation. Users choose a full-length curated soundtrack or a live engine that generates sound as the video plays. The app reads frames at 384x192 pixels and divides them into 8 west-to-east strips. Colour mappings are specific to each animation: white can represent ice, warm colours fire, and small bright dots city lights. Logos, dates and legends are masked out.

In the default Rhythm mode, the amount of a feature in each strip controls beats and loudness. Sound moves west to east, from left to right, with chords and bass. Curated tracks use a fixed scale across the animation. Live engines read video 4 times per second and use only frames already shown during playback. Users can open their own NASA video without uploading it. A separate section turns September Arctic sea-ice extent from 1979-2026 into sound and lets users compare two years.

Benefits

The app adds an audible way to explore information usually presented visually, including for blind and low-vision people. Screen-reader text explains what is sounding and where. Full keyboard control, large touch targets, phone layouts and English and Chinese interfaces offer different ways to use it. On the sea-ice map, touching ice plays a high note, open water a low note, and land stays silent. A narrated guided listen explains the map. Android vibration provides another cue.

Intended impact

The goal is to help people explore shrinking sea ice, spreading fires and changing city lights by ear, using devices they already own. The app has not yet been tested with blind or low-vision users. Testing with these users is the next step.

Tools used

I developed the project as a high school student working alone. The app uses JavaScript, HTML, CSS, Web Audio API and Tone.js. Python, NumPy and FFmpeg support analysis and rendering; Node.js, Playwright and axe-core support testing. Piano methods use Salamander samples and public-domain Debussy scores from Mutopia.

ACE-Step generated AI-music candidates. VoxCPM2 generated narration from a text description without cloning anyone's voice. Meta Audiobox-Aesthetics scored candidate sound quality. Rendering and scoring ran on NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPUs. The open-source app is hosted on GitHub Pages.

What makes it creative

AI music scored highest on the automatic information measure, but I found it hardest to interpret by ear. This changed the selection rule: first require enough information, including on unseen animations, then rank by sound quality. Seven methods were compared: piano sweep, image-as-score, ambient voices, nature sounds, AI music, rhythm and a hybrid. A benchmark on 12 animations measured how well a machine listener could recover data patterns from audio, alongside predicted sound quality. Every method was then tested unchanged on 12 unseen animations. Piano sweep and image-as-score performed worse and were excluded from selection.

Four listening rounds produced 178 answers from one listener: me. Method names were hidden, order randomized and loudness matched. Rhythm won all three of its first-round pairings. Across rounds, quantity comparisons were correct 33 of 48 times (69%, p = 0.007). Left/right position was at chance, so it remains a secondary cue and is also described in words.

Factors considered

The mapping must stay understandable and honest. The app reads colours rather than underlying measurements, so it conveys approximate amount and position, not exact values. Listening evidence is limited to one person. Privacy and licensing also shaped the design. Own-video processing stays in the browser, with no uploads, accounts or tracking. NASA public-domain visuals and open-licensed tools and assets are used.

Playwright tested modes, controls, sound, synchronization and layouts at 320, 375, 768 and 1280 px widths. The axe-core WCAG 2.1 A and AA audit found 0 errors. All 125 rendered soundtracks were checked for loudness and peaks. Earlier sea-ice features and an EIC prototype were built before the weekend with local organizers' permission. The jukebox, seven methods, benchmark, listening tests, live engines, demo and site were built during the hackathon.
